'''Llewellyn Hilleth Thomas''' (21 October 1903 – 20 April 1992) was a British [[physicist]] and [[applied mathematics|applied mathematician]].<ref>{{cite journal|author=Price, Peter J.|title=Obituary: Llewellyn H. Thomas|journal=Physics Today|date=September 1994|volume=47|issue=9|pages=115–116|doi=10.1063/1.2808649|doi-access=free}}</ref> He is best known for his contributions to atomic and molecular physics and solid-state physics. His key achievements include calculating relativistic effects on the [[spin-orbit interaction]] in a [[hydrogenic atom]] ([[Thomas precession]]), creating an approximate theory of <math>N</math>-body quantum systems ([[Thomas-Fermi theory]]), and devising an efficient method for solving tridiagonal system of linear equations ([[Thomas algorithm]]).

== Life and education ==
Born in London, he studied at [[University of Cambridge|Cambridge University]], receiving his [[Bachelor of Arts|BA]], [[PhD]], and [[Master of Arts|MA]] degrees in 1924, 1927 and 1928 respectively.  While on a Traveling Fellowship for the academic year 1925–1926 at [[Niels Bohr Institute|Bohr's Institute in Copenhagen]], he proposed Thomas precession in 1926, to explain the difference between predictions made by spin-orbit coupling theory and experimental observations.

In 1929 he obtained a job as a professor of physics at the [[Ohio State University]], where he stayed until 1943. He married  Naomi Estelle Frech in 1933.<ref name="NASMemoir">{{cite journal|author=Jackson, John David|author-link=John David Jackson (physicist)|year=2009|title=Llewellyn Hilleth Thomas 1903 — 1992|url=http://physics.columbia.edu/files/physics/content/LHThomas.pdf|url-status=dead|journal=Biographical Memoirs|location=Washington, D.C.|publisher=National Academy of Sciences|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160304102312/http://physics.columbia.edu/files/physics/content/LHThomas.pdf|archive-date=2016-03-04|access-date=2014-08-09}}</ref> In 1935 he was the master's thesis advisor for [[Leonard I. Schiff|Leonard Schiff]], whose thesis was published with Thomas as coauthor.<ref name="Bloch">
{{Citation|last=Bloch|first=Felix|chapter=LEONARD ISAAC SCHIFF|chapter-url=http://books.nap.edu/openbook.php?record_id=577&page=300|title=Biographical Memoirs|volume=54|pages=300–323|year=1983|place=Washington, D.C.|publisher=[[National Academies Press|National Academy Press]]|isbn=0-309-03391-8|author-link=Felix Bloch}}</ref> From 1943 until 1945 Thomas worked on ballistics at the [[Aberdeen Proving Ground]] in Maryland.  In 1946 he became a member of the staff of the [[Thomas J. Watson Research Center#Overview|Watson Scientific Computing Laboratory]] at Columbia University, remaining there until 1968. In 1958 he was elected as a member of the [[United States National Academy of Sciences|National Academy of Sciences]]. In 1963, Thomas was appointed as IBM's First Fellow in the Watson Research Center.<ref>{{cite web|date=30 January 2012|title=IBM - IBM Fellows|url=http://www.ibm.com/ibm/ideasfromibm/us/ibm_fellows/directory/|website=www.ibm.com}}</ref> He was appointed professor at [[North Carolina State University]] in 1968, retiring from this position in 1976.<ref name="NASMemoir" /> In 1982 he received the [[Davisson–Germer Prize in Atomic or Surface Physics|Davisson-Germer Prize]].<ref>{{cite web|title=Llewellyn Thomas, Array of Contermporary American Physicists|url=http://www.aip.org/history/acap/biographies/bio.jsp?thomasl}}</ref> He died in Raleigh, North Carolina.<ref name="NASMemoir" /><ref>{{cite web|author=Jackson, John David|date=14 Feb 2010|title=Llewellyn Hilleth Thomas 1903 – 1992|url=http://apps3.aps.org/aps/meetings/april10/presentations/H10-3-Jackson.pdf}}</ref>

== Contributions ==
Thomas was responsible for multiple advances in physics. The Thomas precession is a correction to the atomic [[spin-orbit interaction]] in [[quantum mechanics]], which takes into account the [[Special relativity|relativistic]] [[time dilation]] between the [[electron]] and the [[atomic nucleus]]. The Thomas–Fermi model is a statistical model for electron-[[ion]] interactions, which later formed the basis of [[density functional theory]]. The Thomas collapse is effect in [[Few-body systems|few-body physics]], which corresponds to infinite value of the three body [[binding energy]] for zero-range potentials.

In mathematics, his name is frequently attached to an efficient [[Gaussian elimination]] method for [[Tridiagonal matrix|tridiagonal matrices]]—the Thomas algorithm.
